name: Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: World Health Organization (WHO) Diagnostic Criteria for Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis

criteria.description: Angiocentric and angiodestructive lymphoid infiltrates with necrosis on biopsy
Presence of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive B cells demonstrated by in situ hybridization
Pulmonary nodules or infiltrates on imaging consistent with lymphomatoid granulomatosis
Exclusion of other lymphoproliferative disorders and vasculitides
Immunophenotyping showing mixed T-cell and EBV-positive B-cell infiltrates

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Histopathologic evidence of angiocentric lymphoid infiltrates with EBV-positive B cells plus compatible clinical and radiologic pulmonary findings, excluding other lymphomas or vasculitis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires tissue biopsy; clinical and radiologic correlation is essential.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Pulmonary nodules with angiocentric necrotizing infiltrates
searchTerms: lung nodules with blood vessel-centered tissue death

pathognomonic.notes: Detected by in situ hybridization on biopsy

searchTerms: cough with or without coughing blood
losing weight and sweating at night

common.symptomName: Skin lesions including erythematous papules or nodules
Neurological deficits due to CNS involvement
searchTerms: neurological signs due to CNS disease
eye problems including inflammation inside the eye
eye involvement with redness and pain
kidney problems from blood vessel inflammation
kidney damage caused by vessel inflammation

laboratory: Presence of EBV DNA in tissue samples
imaging: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with cavitation on chest CT
Brain MRI showing multifocal lesions in CNS involvement
genetic: No specific germline mutations identified; EBV association is key
other: Histopathology showing angiocentric and angiodestructive lymphoid infiltrates with necrosis
Immunohistochemistry positive for CD20+ B cells and EBV-encoded RNA (EBER)

distinguishingFeatures: Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without EBV positivity
More frequent upper respiratory tract involvement
Predominantly CNS involvement without systemic pulmonary nodules
Lack of angiocentric necrosis typical of lymphomatoid granulomatosis
Strong association with EBV but different histopathology
Commonly involves nasal cavity and upper aerodigestive tract

redFlags: Rapidly progressive pulmonary nodules with cavitation
Neurological deterioration with multifocal CNS lesions
Failure to respond to standard immunosuppressive therapy
references: Swerdlow SH, Campo E, Harris NL, et al. WHO Classification of Tumours of Haematopoietic and Lymphoid Tissues. IARC; 2017.
